A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
both models perform well in forecasting key macroeconomic variables, and that the choice of the model depends on the specific variable of interest.

the Stock and Watson model outperforms the Forni et al. model in terms of forecasting accuracy for the unemployment rate, while the Forni model outperforms Stock and Watson for industrial production and consumer price inflation.

the Stock and Watson model outperforms the Forni et al.'s in terms of forecasting the unemployment rate, while the latter model outperforms in terms of forecasting industrial production, consumer prices, and the PMI, but only for a subset of the variables and only for some of the forecast horizons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of the factor model to use for nowcasting depends on the variable of interest.
the choice of a factor model should be based on the particular forecasting application at hand.
the forecasting performance of dynamic factor models depends on the specific dataset and the variables of interest, suggesting the need for further work on model selection and model combination.
